newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel unity government good for economy - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Israel unity government good for economy - analysts.

text.p: Israel's ailing economy would benefit from a national unity government under consideration by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, analysts said on Wednesday.
"It would be great but I can't see it happening. Even within the Labour (opposition) party many have problems with it," said Gidi Halperin, investment director at Meitav Investments and Securities.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday he was weighing the possibility of forming a unity government to achieve a broad consensus for a final peace deal with the Palestinians.
"I am definitely considering it but I have not taken any decision on the matter," he told Israeli Army Radio.
Talk of a unity government has grown as negotiations with the Palestinians plunged into a crisis after Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem last month.
A unity government would help lift pressure from Netanyahu's current far-right coalition partners over peace negotiations.
It could also aid a slowing economy.

"I think the biggest spinoff on the economy of a unity government is not so much on economic policy, but more so on the general atmosphere it will create that the peace process is ongoing. Foreign investors are sort of having doubts now," said Jonathan Katz, senior economist at Solid Financial Markets.
The signing of a peace accord with the Palestinians in 1993 opened up new markets for Israel, boosted tourism and unleashed a flood of foreign investment.
All this is at risk just as Israel's economy teeters on the brink of a recession.
A unity government would give Netanyahu a broad parliamentary base to implement economic reform.

"In order to affect positive changes and curtail the negative trends that have come to dominate the economy, Israel's leadership must posses the kind of political sway that Benjamin Netanyahu currently lacks," business columnist Avraham Tal wrote last week in the Jerusalem Post.
"A broad government...can promote Israel's economic agenda better than a narrow government besieged by a strong opposition," Tal said.
After five years of rapid growth economists are forecasting zero expansion in per capita gross domestic product this year.

Finance Minister Dan Meridor has been unable to persuade the inflation-fighting central bank to lower interest rates to boost activity. Nor has he succeeded in propelling the economy to the top of the national agenda.
It comes as no surprise, therefore, that the moderate Meridor is one of the biggest boosters of unity government from within Netanyahu's Likud party.
"I thought from the day we won the elections and Netanyahu was chosen prime minister, it was right to make an effort to set up a broad government," Meridor told Israel Radio last week.
Katz noted that it was a coalition government in 1985 that pulled Israel out of one of its worst economic crises.

Current Labour Party leader Shimon Peres, serving then as finance minister, spearheaded a stabilisation programme that tackled hyperinflation of more than 400 percent a year and paved the way for the boom of the 1990s.

A new unity government would likely spark a stock market rally, at least at first. Activity on the Tel Aviv market has dwindled lately as foreign investors remain sidelined, awaiting a positive sign on the peace front.
"Initially, such a government would pull the wagon out of the mud," Halperin said.
"But if after two weeks government members are already fighting and not accomplishing anything, investors won't like that."
